title: What is known about 1RB1LD_1RC1RE_1LA0RA_1RC0LB_0LA1RF_---1RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LD_1RC1RE_1LA0RA_1RC0LB_0LA1RF_---1RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and the run is now an explicit map. Read in cell pairs, the tape is a bit string. The run is a base-4 countdown on its blocks 010: separators pass borrows along like the digits of a counter, and the block grown at the near end becomes the new timer at each overflow. Nine rules, the ticks and two overflows, are proved in Lean. The map reproduces every tick boundary of the first 6·109 steps exactly, and runs on to 1.0·1019 steps without a halting event. Halting could only come from the far end once its last block wears away. The machine writes exactly the same tape as 1RB1LD_1RC1RF_1LA1RD_1RE0LB_---0RA_0LA1RC for at least 109 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 50,611 cells have been visited and 39,628 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: The ticks
claims.text: From 0^∞ 1110 (111110)^(n+1) 1 A> (101110)^x SEP …, one tick reaches the same form with n+2, and the separator after the first block (the timer) moves one step along r = 10 → q = 1110 → p = 101011 → s = 11 → r: r → q costs the next block one, q → p costs the timer one, p → s changes nothing, s → r costs the timer one, gives the next block one and passes a borrow on. Also the wall cycle: with a timer of one followed by s, three ticks take two from the next block and pass no borrow. Every n, every block length, every tape to the right.

claims.title: Overflow, for two and three blocks
claims.text: When every separator is s and the far end reads 1111, the borrow runs to the far end. From one tick boundary to the next, the list (n+1; x1, …, xk) becomes (6; n+2, x1−1, x2−1, x3, …) with separators r, q, r, … and far end 10101111: the grown w-block is the new timer. Proved for k = 2 and k = 3, for all n and block lengths.

claims.title: An exact map reproduces the run
claims.text: Read the tape right of the head in cell pairs 1b → b. The run is then a map on (n, word): the ticks above as rewrites of the bits, the other phase of a tick (01 W moves as W), the wall, and events (a borrow at the far end, a timer running out), which are computed by running the machine on a copy with every block cut to 40 copies and lifted back. Each event is computed with two cuts, which must agree. In the first 6·109 steps the map reproduces all 22,198 tick boundaries of the machine exactly: n, the word and the step count. 53 of these moves are events.

claims.title: Same tape as its twin
claims.text: This machine and 1RB1LD_1RC1RF_1LA1RD_1RE0LB_---0RA_0LA1RC write the same symbol at the same cell and move the same way at every one of the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps. Where one is in C, the other is in C or E, depending on the symbol under the head. They stay twins as long as three local patterns hold: after B reads 0 the next cell is 0, after D reads 0 it is 1, and after E reads 1 it is 1.

claims.title: The map runs on to 1.0·10<sup>19</sup> steps
claims.text: From the first tick boundary, the map runs 627,024,786 ticks to step 10,230,187,408,184,952,134 with 205 events. Both cuts agree at every event, and no cut copy halts. The first 400 moves by the other phase and by the wall were also compared with the machine. The run meets 89 overflows; the largest new timers are 4,194,301 (at 1.1·10<sup>15</sup>), 33,628,307 (at 2.2·10<sup>16</sup>), 129,459,917 (at 3.3·10<sup>17</sup>), 416,954,747 (at 3.5·10<sup>18</sup>). At the end the list is 1, 222,014,566, 1, 612,354, 493, 644, 9,920, 1,002.

claims.title: The overflow formulas
claims.text: Every overflow the map meets follows one of two formulas: 74 times F1 (all separators s, far end 11: (n; x1, …) → (6; n+1, x1−1, x2−1, x3, …)) and 15 times F2 (the timer runs out at a q: (n; 1, x1, …) → (6; n, x1+1, x2−1, …)).

claims.title: The far end cannot halt while the last block lasts
claims.text: A borrow arriving at the far end halts the machine when the far end reads 01, 101, 1101 and a few similar words. The 102 far ends seen in 6·109 steps close under borrow arrivals into 128 far ends, none of which halts. All of them fall into the cycle 11 → overflow → 0011 → 11, where the last block loses one per overflow. This assumes that a far end behaves the same behind any block of 10 or more copies.

claims.title: Why it is hard
claims.text: Block i, counted from the timer, loses about 2·4<sup>-(i+1)</sup> per tick, so the far end is reached exponentially rarely, and the last block (1,002 at the end of the long run) wears down by one per overflow. Halting is only possible at an event, once the far end has changed shape.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The open part is what the list looks like once its last blocks have worn away, and whether a far end like …01 can then appear.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine runs a countdown on a list of blocks of the word 101110. The short words between blocks act like the digits of a base-4 counter, passing borrows along, while a block at the near end of the tape keeps growing. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the countdown. Its moves are proved in Lean for every block length. It has a twin, 1RB1LD_1RC1RF_1LA1RD_1RE0LB_---0RA_0LA1RC, which writes exactly the same tape.

facts.text: Ticks, the wall cycle and two overflows, for every block length, proved in Lean.
Tick boundaries in the first 6·10<sup>9</sup> steps that the map reproduces exactly.
Steps the map has run without a halting event.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 50,611 cells (38,691 left of the start, 51 right), with a density of 1s of 0.783.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A growing block, a timer and separators
html: Watch the head when it turns in state A just past the near end of the tape. The tape reads 1110 (111110)^n 1 A> (101110)^x1 s1 (101110)^x2 s2 …. The block of w = 111110 grows by two copies every tick. The blocks of v = 101110 form the countdown, and the first one, x1, is the timer.
The separators are r = 10, q = 1110, p = 101011 and s = 11. Each tick moves the separator after the timer one step along the cycle r → q → p → s → r:
<div style="overflow-x:auto"><table class="tbl"><thead><tr><th>separator</th><th>becomes</th><th>blocks</th><th>Lean</th></tr></thead><tbody>
r 10qthe block after it −1tick_r
q 1110pthe block before it −1tick_q
p 101011snonetick_p
s 11rbefore −1, after +1, and a borrow moves on to the next separatortick_s

A borrow arriving at any later separator does the same. So each separator is a base-4 digit. The block before a separator loses 2 per full cycle of that separator, and the block after it loses one and gets it back.

sections.heading: A base-4 countdown
html: The timer loses 2 units every 4 ticks. Its separator passes every fourth borrow to the next one, which passes every fourth of those, and so on. Block i, counted from the timer, loses about 2·4-(i+1) per tick, while the w-block grows by 2. Here are eight consecutive tick starts, from step 1,423,348:
<div style="overflow-x:auto"><table class="tbl"><thead><tr><th>step</th><th>timer, separator, next blocks</th></tr></thead><tbody>
1,472,8307 r 65 r 12 s 39 (two s pass the borrow on)
In the first 3·108 steps, all 3,409 ticks whose borrow stays inside the standard blocks follow this rule exactly.

sections.heading: An exact map
html: Read the tape right of the head in cell pairs: every pair starts with a 1, and the pair 1b stands for the bit b. A block of v is 010, and the separators r, q, p, s are 0, 10, 001, 1. The four ticks become rewrites of bits: r → q is 0 010 → 10, q → p is 010 10 → 001, p → s drops a 00, and s → r is 010 1 → 0010 followed by a borrow. Written this way they also cover the separators that appear when a block in the middle runs out, such as 10001. A tick costs 72n + 6j + 182 + 4m (+10 when it ends with q → p) steps, where j is where the borrow stops and m the number of s → r.

Two more moves complete it. A word 01 W is the same tick half a step later, and moves as W does. The wall 0101 v^x (a timer of one and an s) takes two from the next block every three ticks and passes no borrow. The long run makes 185,236,728 wall moves.

What is left are events. The main one is the overflow: when every separator is s, the borrow runs to the far end. Then the list (n; x1, …, xk) becomes (6; n+1, x1−1, x2−1, x3, …): the w-block grown at the near end is the new timer, which is why new timers are close to powers of 4. This is proved in Lean for two and three blocks. The other events are computed by running the machine on a copy of the tape with every block cut to 40 copies. Each event is computed twice with different cuts, and the two results must agree.

Against the real machine, this map reproduces all 22,198 tick boundaries of the first 6·109 steps exactly, including the step counts. Run on its own, it reaches 1.0·1019 steps without a halting event.

The machine can halt only when a borrow reaches a far end that reads …01 or a few similar words. Every far end the run has shown leads, under further borrows, into the cycle 11 → 0011, which does not halt. In that cycle the last block loses one per overflow. So halting could only come after the last block, now 1,002, has worn away, and the far end is reached ever more rarely.

sections.heading: Two machines, one tape
html: 1RB1LD_1RC1RE_1LA0RA_1RC0LB_0LA1RF_---1RD and 1RB1LD_1RC1RF_1LA1RD_1RE0LB_---0RA_0LA1RC are different tables, but from a blank tape they write the same symbol at the same cell and move the same way at every step checked, 109 of them. Their states correspond one to one except that state C of one machine is split between C and E of the other, according to the symbol under the head. The correspondence holds as long as three local patterns hold: after B reads 0 the next cell is 0, after D reads 0 it is 1, and after E reads 1 it is 1. The same Lean statements are proved for both.

summary: A base-4 countdown on a list of blocks of 101110, now an exact map on (n, word) that reproduces every tick boundary of the first 6e9 steps and runs on to 1.0·10^19 steps; it writes the same tape as 1RB1LD_1RC1RF_1LA1RD_1RE0LB_---0RA_0LA1RC.
